title: 9/5/2026 | JOHN B. BRADLEY - LAZY S RANCH | PC | Pro se intervenor requests PUC accept the PFD and deny the Applications for CCN given mandatory notice and public-participation requirements were not met, the Commission’s rules must mean what they say, and they must be accountability.

=== FINAL PUBLIC COMMENT - John B. Bradley.pdf ===
PUBLIC COMMENT — PUC DOCKET NO. 59475

Re: Joint Application of Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission
Service Corporation for the Bell County East Switch to Big Hill 765-kV Transmission
Line Project

I respectfully ask the Commission to accept the Administrative Law Judges’ Proposal for
Decision (PFD) and deny the Applications because the Applicants failed to provide the
notice and public participation required by the Texas Administrative Code.

My exception to the PFD was intentionally short and simple: Simply accept the PFD and
deny the Application due to failure of adequate notification.

The reason is straightforward. The PFD correctly recognizes that the Applicants did not
comply with 16 TAC §22.52(a)(3), governing notice of the Application, and 16 TAC
§22.52(a)(4), governing the required public participation meeting. These are separate
requirements serving different purposes. They should not be treated as
interchangeable.

An opportunity for a person to intervene after an application has been filed is not
equivalent to the opportunity required by the Commission’s rules to participate in the
pre-application public meeting process and community-values period.

That distinction matters. The notice and participation requirements exist to give affected
communities an opportunity to learn about a proposed project and provide input at the
stage contemplated by the Commission’s rules—not merely to give property owners an
opportunity to enter a contested case after the application is already before the
Commission.

The Commission should not treat a later opportunity to intervene as a cure

If the Applicants failed to satisfy the requirements of §§22.52(a)(3) and 22.52(a)(4), the
Commission should address that failure directly. A later opportunity to intervene does
not necessarily cure a failure to provide the earlier notice and public participation
opportunity required by rule.

The Commission should therefore explain, on the record, what legal authority permits a
failure to comply with those mandatory notice and participation requirements to be
excused or cured after the fact.

Concern regarding the Commission’s role and the appearance of a predetermined
outcome

The Commission is the decision-maker. Commission Staff and the parties may properly
submit pleadings, exceptions, recommendations, and evidence within the administrative
process. My concern is that a preponderance of PUC-related submissions and
 recommendations in the record appear to align with positions advanced by the
Applicants. Most notably, Commission Staff may make recommendations concerning
preferred routes or other outcomes that can reasonably be understood as favoring
approval of the project before the Commissioners themselves have made a final
determination.

There is an important distinction between objectively evaluating the record and making
recommendations that effectively identify a preferred route or outcome. When
Commission Staff recommends a particular route, rather than limiting its analysis to
whether proposed routes satisfy the applicable statutory and regulatory criteria, that
recommendation can reasonably create the appearance that approval of the project is
already assumed and that the remaining question is merely which route should be
selected.

I am not accusing any individual Commissioner or member of Commission Staff of
prejudging this docket. I am asking the Commission to recognize the appearance
problem created when the agency’s own submissions substantially align with the
Applicants’ requested outcome and include recommendations that infer approval before
the Commissioners formally vote. The Commission should address that concern
through a transparent, objective, and independently reasoned decision based on the
evidentiary record, the ALJs’ findings, and the governing law.

The public should be able to see that the Commissioners independently considered the
ALJs’ findings, the parties’ exceptions, the evidence, and the governing law—and that
the final decision was not predetermined.

Chairman Gleeson’s prior memorandum makes this especially important

I raised this issue now because Chairman Gleeson’s prior memorandum in another
docket demonstrated why intervenors should not simply assume that an ALJ’s PFD will
be adopted as written.

That memorandum was issued in a different docket, and I recognize that the
Commission is not bound by the outcome or reasoning of that proceeding.
Nevertheless, the memorandum raised substantial concerns about the weight given to
the ALJs’ recommendations and the role of the Commission in modifying their
conclusions.

For that reason, my exception was intentionally preemptive. I wanted the record in
Docket No. 59475 to make clear that, if the Commission intends to reject the ALJs’
findings concerning the Applicants’ failure to comply with the notice and public-
participation requirements, the Commission should explain precisely why those TAC
requirements do not require denial of the Applications.

A policy disagreement with the ALJs cannot substitute for compliance with the governing
rules. What happens if the Commission approves the Applications despite these
 findings? This is also why the Commission should consider carefully what precedent it
establishes.

If the Commission approves the Applications despite the PFD’s findings concerning
violations of §§22.52(a)(3) and 22.52(a)(4), affected pro se intervenors will have to
consider the remedies available under Texas administrative law.

Those remedies may include seeking judicial review of the Commission’s final order and
asking the reviewing court to reverse or remand the decision if the statutory standards
are met—including where the decision is affected by unlawful procedure, error of law,
action in excess of statutory authority, lack of substantial evidence, or arbitrary or
capricious action. Texas Government Code §2001.174 provides the framework for that
judicial review.

Accordingly, if the Commission rejects the PFD and approves the Applications, I
respectfully request that the final order:

   Identify and address each finding concerning the Applicants’ compliance with 16 TAC
§22.52(a)(3) and §22.52(a)(4);
   Explain whether the Commission finds that the Applicants complied with each
requirement and, if not, identify the legal authority for nevertheless approving the
Applications;
   Explain why a post-application opportunity to intervene is legally sufficient, if that is
the Commission’s position, to address the separate pre-application notice and public-
participation requirements;
   Identify the evidence supporting any rejection of the ALJs’ findings;
   Clearly state the Commission’s independent reasoning rather than merely adopting
an Applicant or Staff position; and
   Preserve a complete and understandable record for any affected intervenor seeking
administrative or judicial review.

Accountability

Finally, I respectfully ask a simple question that should matter to every participant in this
proceeding:

If the Applicants violated mandatory TAC requirements, and the Commission
nevertheless approves the CCN without requiring those requirements to be satisfied,
who is accountable for that decision, and what remedy is available to the affected
landowners and pro se intervenors?

Applicants should not receive the benefit of a CCN while disregarding requirements
imposed by the Commission’s own rules. And the Commission should not create the
impression that its rules are mandatory for the public but optional when compliance
would interfere with approval of a major transmission project.
 The appropriate and simplest resolution is available: Accept the PFD and deny the
Applications for failure to provide the notice and public participation required by 16 TAC
§§22.52(a)(3) and 22.52(a)(4).

Respectfully submitted,

/s/ John B. Bradley
John B. Bradley
Lazy S Ranch
Pro Se Intervenor
PUC Docket No. 59475
